newsitem.title: USA: Black athletes with heart problem at higher risk.
newsitem.headline: Black athletes with heart problem at higher risk.

text.p: Young, black athletes with a rare heart condition are more at risk of dying from it on the athletic field because of a lack of access to adequate medical care, a study presented on Wednesday said.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a thickening of the left ventricle wall that can cause the heart to beat out of control and result in instant death.

The genetic disorder occurs in about one in 500 people. Most who have it are unaware of it, but it is the most common cause of sudden death among children and adolescents, Dr. Barry Maron of the Minneapolis Heart Institute said at an American College of Cardiology conference.

Young, black athletes die from it during sporting events in greater numbers than their white counterparts because blacks are less likely to know they suffer from the condition and should avoid over-exertion, Maron said.

His study looked at 153 sudden deaths of U.S. athletes over the past 10 years, mostly basketball and football players ranging in age from 16 to 21. Of those, 42 percent suffered from confirmed or possible hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. More than half were black, although blacks comprised fewer than half the total group of sudden death victims.
"The disease has always been there ... but the diagnosis is not being made among African-Americans. As a result, these individuals are not being withdrawn from competition," Maron said.
The problem is one of access to adequate medical care, especially in the inner city.

"If you are a young African-American male and you don't have a regular doctor, which is often the case, you are going to have less chance of having a diagnosis (of the disorder) made than a suburban child with greater access to testing, such as an echocardiogram," Maron said.

Another study presented at the conference by Dr. Augustus Grant of Duke University Medical Centre underlined the inequities of medical care between blacks and whites in the United States. Blacks were shown in studies done in Nashville, Tennessee, and Chicago to be at least twice as likely as whites to die from sudden heart malfunction, he said.

The screening of young athletes for physical fitness is conducted on a national scale, but it consists usually of a routine physical exam and a family medical history survey, which seldom detect hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Three-quarters of the people who have the condition do not even exhibit a heart murmur, he said.

Requiring would-be competitors to undergo a $600 echocardiography test would likely cut sudden athletic field deaths, but wide adoption of such tests seems unlikely because of costs and logistics, Maron said.
Sudden death may be seen most often in basketball and football due to the popularity of those sports. "But some of it may be the sports themselves," Maron said.

In his study, he said, few deaths were found among distance runners, soccer players and other athletes whose exertion levels were more prolonged. Football and basketball require short bursts of strenuous activity, which are the most likely to trigger abnormal heart rhythms, he said.
He dismissed the notion that athletes can somehow push themselves too hard, literally running themselves to death.
"That's a myth," Maron said. "These are young individuals who surprisingly can compete at high levels while harbouring, unknown to them, a basic structural abnormality of the heart."
